3.1.goal: Build the probability distribution (PMF) of the sum of two dice as a table, find its mean and variance from the PMF, and check them by simulation.

blocks.title: The PMF as a table
blocks.text: We count how many of the 36 equally likely pairs give each sum, then divide by 36. A pandas table keeps the values, the counts and the probabilities side by side.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from itertools import product

sums = [a + b for a, b in product(range(1, 7), repeat=2)]
pmf = pd.Series(sums).value_counts().sort_index() / 36

table = pd.DataFrame({'ways': (pmf * 36).astype(int), 'P(X = x)': pmf.round(4)})
table.index.name = 'sum x'
print(table.to_string())

blocks.title: Check it is a valid PMF and add the CDF
blocks.text: A valid PMF has probabilities between 0 and 1 that add to exactly 1. The running total (cumsum) is the CDF, which answers 'at most' questions at once.
blocks.code:
print('total probability:', round(pmf.sum(), 10))

cdf = pmf.cumsum()
print(f'P(X <= 4)  = {cdf[4]:.4f}')
print(f'P(X >= 10) = {1 - cdf[9]:.4f}')

blocks.title: Mean and variance from the PMF
blocks.text: The mean is the sum of x times P(x). The variance is the sum of (x minus the mean) squared times P(x). These describe the whole population of possible rolls, so there is no n - 1 here.
blocks.code:
x = pmf.index.to_numpy()
p = pmf.to_numpy()

mean = (x * p).sum()
var = ((x - mean) ** 2 * p).sum()

print(f'mean     = {mean:.4f}')
print(f'variance = {var:.4f}')
print(f'sd       = {var ** 0.5:.4f}')

blocks.title: Check by simulation
blocks.text: Roll two dice 100,000 times with a seeded generator. The simulated mean and variance should sit close to the exact ones. ddof=0 matches the population formula above.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=100_000) + rng.integers(1, 7, size=100_000)

print(f'simulated mean     = {rolls.mean():.4f}')
print(f'simulated variance = {rolls.var(ddof=0):.4f}')
print(f'simulated P(X = 7) = {(rolls == 7).mean():.4f}  (exact {pmf[7]:.4f})')

r.code:
s <- as.vector(outer(1:6, 1:6, "+"))
pmf <- table(s) / 36
x <- as.numeric(names(pmf))
round(pmf, 4)
mu <- sum(x * pmf)
mu
sum((x - mu)^2 * pmf)
sqrt(sum((x - mu)^2 * pmf))

set.seed(42)
rolls <- sample(6, 1e5, TRUE) + sample(6, 1e5, TRUE)
c(mean(rolls), mean((rolls - mean(rolls))^2))
r.expect: mean 7; variance 5.8333; sd 2.4152; P(X = 7) = 0.1667; the simulated mean and variance are close to 7 and 5.83
r.note: These are the population formulas, matching Python. R's var() would divide by n - 1, so for the simulation we square the gaps ourselves. Simulated values are close, not identical.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies (Statistics: Mean, Variance)
spss.syntax:
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP #a = 1 TO 6.
LOOP #b = 1 TO 6.
COMPUTE total = #a + #b.
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=total
  /STATISTICS=MEAN VARIANCE STDDEV.
spss.note: The Percent column is the PMF (for example 16.7 for a sum of 7) and Cumulative Percent is the CDF. The mean is 7.00. SPSS divides by n - 1 = 35, so it reports variance 6.000; multiply by 35/36 to get the population value 5.8333.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 36
gen total = ceil(_n/6) + mod(_n - 1, 6) + 1
tabulate total
summarize total
display r(Var) * 35/36

clear
set seed 42
set obs 100000
gen rolls = ceil(6*runiform()) + ceil(6*runiform())
summarize rolls
stata.note: tabulate gives the PMF as the Percent column and Cum. as the CDF. summarize uses n - 1, so r(Var) is 6; times 35/36 gives the population variance 5.8333. The simulation is close to 7 but not identical to Python's.

3.2.goal: Use the binomial distribution for the lesson's drug that works for 70% of patients (10 patients): exactly, at most and at least, plus mean, SD and a simulation check.

blocks.title: Exactly 7 respond
blocks.text: binom.pmf(k, n, p) gives P(X = k), one bar of the distribution. We also compute the lesson's formula C(n, k) x p^k x (1 - p)^(n - k) by hand to see that they agree.
blocks.code:
import math
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binom

n, p = 10, 0.7

by_hand = math.comb(n, 7) * p**7 * (1 - p)**3
print(f'formula   : {by_hand:.4f}')
print(f'binom.pmf : {binom.pmf(7, n, p):.4f}')

blocks.title: At most, more than, at least
blocks.text: cdf(k) is P(X <= k), 'at most k'. sf(k) is the survival function P(X > k), 'more than k'. So 'at least 9' is sf(8), which is the same as 1 minus cdf(8).
blocks.code:
print(f'P(X <= 6)  at most 6      = {binom.cdf(6, n, p):.4f}')
print(f'P(X > 8)   more than 8      = {binom.sf(8, n, p):.4f}')
print(f'P(X >= 9)  at least 9       = {1 - binom.cdf(8, n, p):.4f}')
print(f'P(9) + P(10) added by hand  = {binom.pmf(9, n, p) + binom.pmf(10, n, p):.4f}')

blocks.title: Mean and standard deviation
blocks.text: The shortcuts are mean = n x p and SD = square root of n x p x (1 - p). SciPy's stats method returns the same values from the distribution itself.
blocks.code:
print(f'mean = n*p = {n * p:.1f}')
print(f'variance   = {n * p * (1 - p):.2f}')
print(f'SD         = {math.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)):.3f}')

m, v = binom.stats(n, p)
print(f'scipy      : mean {float(m):.1f}, variance {float(v):.2f}')

blocks.title: Check by simulation
blocks.text: Run the 10-patient trial 100,000 times with a seeded generator and count how many responders each trial has. The simulated shares should be close to the exact probabilities.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
responders = rng.binomial(n, p, size=100_000)

print(f'simulated P(X = 7)  = {(responders == 7).mean():.4f}  (exact {binom.pmf(7, n, p):.4f})')
print(f'simulated P(X >= 9) = {(responders >= 9).mean():.4f}  (exact {binom.sf(8, n, p):.4f})')
print(f'simulated mean {responders.mean():.3f}, SD {responders.std():.3f}')

r.code:
n <- 10; p <- 0.7
dbinom(7, n, p)                       # exactly 7
pbinom(6, n, p)                       # at most 6
pbinom(8, n, p, lower.tail = FALSE)   # more than 8 = at least 9
n * p
sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))

set.seed(42)
x <- rbinom(100000, n, p)
mean(x == 7)
r.note: dbinom, pbinom and rbinom are R's pmf, cdf and random draws. lower.tail = FALSE gives the survival probability P(X > k). The simulation is close to the exact value, not identical to Python's.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (Function group: PDF & Noncentral PDF, CDF & Noncentral CDF, Random Numbers)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / dummy.
BEGIN DATA
1
END DATA.
COMPUTE exact7 = PDF.BINOM(7, 10, 0.7).
COMPUTE atmost6 = CDF.BINOM(6, 10, 0.7).
COMPUTE atleast9 = 1 - CDF.BINOM(8, 10, 0.7).
COMPUTE mean_x = 10 * 0.7.
COMPUTE sd_x = SQRT(10 * 0.7 * 0.3).
FORMATS exact7 atmost6 atleast9 sd_x (F8.4).
LIST VARIABLES=exact7 atmost6 atleast9 mean_x sd_x.
spss.note: PDF.BINOM(k, n, p) is the pmf and CDF.BINOM(k, n, p) is P(X <= k). For a simulation use COMPUTE x = RV.BINOM(10, 0.7) on many cases; the result is close to, not identical to, Python's.

stata.code:
display binomialp(10, 7, 0.7)
display binomial(10, 6, 0.7)
display binomialtail(10, 9, 0.7)
display 10 * 0.7
display sqrt(10 * 0.7 * 0.3)

clear
set seed 42
set obs 100000
gen x = rbinomial(10, 0.7)
gen is7 = (x == 7)
summarize is7
stata.note: In Stata binomialp(n, k, p) is P(X = k), binomial(n, k, p) is P(X <= k) and binomialtail(n, k, p) is P(X >= k), so 'at least 9' uses k = 9. The simulated mean of is7 is close to 0.2668, not identical to Python's.

3.3.goal: Use the emergency room's average of 4 arrivals per hour to find the chance of exactly 2 arrivals and of a rush of 8 or more.

blocks.title: Set the average rate
blocks.text: The Poisson distribution only needs one number: the average count per interval, called lambda. The ER averages 4 arrivals an hour, so we build a Poisson distribution with that rate.
blocks.code:
from scipy import stats

lam = 4
er = stats.poisson(mu=lam)

print('mean     =', er.mean())
print('variance =', er.var())

blocks.title: Exactly 2 arrivals
blocks.text: pmf gives the probability of one exact count. Notice the mean and the variance are both 4: that equality is the Poisson's fingerprint.
blocks.code:
p2 = er.pmf(2)

print(f'P(X = 2) = {p2:.4f}')

blocks.title: A rush of 8 or more
blocks.text: '8 or more' is everything except 0 to 7. The survival function sf(7) is P(X > 7), which is exactly that, so it is shorter and more accurate than adding eight terms.
blocks.code:
rush = er.sf(7)

print(f'P(X >= 8) = {rush:.4f}')
print(f'about 1 hour in {1 / rush:.0f}')

blocks.title: See the whole distribution
blocks.text: A table of probabilities shows where the mass sits. Most hours bring 2 to 6 patients, and the long right tail is the rare rush.
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

k = list(range(0, 11))
table = pd.DataFrame({'k': k, 'P(X = k)': er.pmf(k).round(4)})

print(table.to_string(index=False))

r.code:
dpois(2, lambda = 4)
1 - ppois(7, lambda = 4)
ppois(7, lambda = 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
r.expect: dpois = 0.1465; 1 - ppois(7, 4) = 0.0511 (the last line gives the same 0.0511)
r.note: dpois is P(X = k), ppois is P(X <= k), and lower.tail = FALSE gives the 'more than' side directly.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (use the PDF.POISSON and CDF.POISSON functions)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / dummy.
BEGIN DATA
1
END DATA.
COMPUTE p_exactly_2 = PDF.POISSON(2, 4).
COMPUTE p_8_or_more = 1 - CDF.POISSON(7, 4).
FORMATS p_exactly_2 p_8_or_more (F8.4).
LIST p_exactly_2 p_8_or_more.
spss.note: SPSS has no Poisson menu, so the Compute Variable dialog with PDF.POISSON(k, lambda) and CDF.POISSON(k, lambda) does the work.

stata.code:

display poissontail(4, 8)
display 1 - poisson(4, 7)
stata.note: poissonp(m,k) is P(X = k) and poissontail(m,k) is P(X >= k), so 8 or more is poissontail(4, 8); poisson(m,k) is P(X <= k).

3.4.goal: Use the heights of adult men (mean 69.1 in, SD 2.9 in) to find the share shorter than 66 inches and the height of the 90th percentile.

blocks.title: Describe the bell curve
blocks.text: A normal distribution is fixed by two numbers: its centre (the mean) and its width (the standard deviation). SciPy bundles both into one object we can ask questions of.
blocks.code:
from scipy import stats

mean, sd = 69.1, 2.9
heights = stats.norm(loc=mean, scale=sd)

print('median =', heights.median())

blocks.title: Share shorter than 66 inches
blocks.text: cdf gives the area under the curve to the left of a value, which is the probability of being at or below it. The z-score says how many standard deviations 66 is below the mean.
blocks.code:
z = (66 - mean) / sd
share = heights.cdf(66)

print(f'z = {z:.2f}')
print(f'P(height < 66) = {share:.4f}')

blocks.title: The 90th percentile
blocks.text: ppf runs the other way: give it an area and it returns the value. Only 10% of men are taller than the height it prints.
blocks.code:
p90 = heights.ppf(0.90)

print(f'90th percentile = {p90:.1f} inches')

blocks.title: Check the 68-95-99.7 rule
blocks.text: The empirical rule says about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean. We check it with the standard normal curve.

blocks.title: Draw it
blocks.text: The shaded area is the probability we computed for men shorter than 66 inches. A picture makes it clear that probabilities are areas.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(mean - 4 * sd, mean + 4 * sd, 300)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.4))
plt.plot(x, heights.pdf(x))
plt.fill_between(x, heights.pdf(x), where=x < 66, alpha=0.4)
plt.xlabel('height (inches)')
plt.show()

r.code:
pnorm(66, mean = 69.1, sd = 2.9)
qnorm(0.90, mean = 69.1, sd = 2.9)
pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)
pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2)
r.note: pnorm gives the area to the left of a value, and qnorm is its inverse.

END DATA.

stata.code:

display 69.1 + 2.9 * invnormal(0.90)

3.5.goal: Use the airline that books 200 people (10% no-shows) to see how well a normal curve approximates the exact binomial answer for fewer than 15 no-shows.

blocks.title: Check the condition
blocks.text: The normal curve is a good stand-in for the binomial only when both np and n(1 - p) are at least 10. Here n = 200 and p = 0.1, so we check both numbers first.
blocks.code:
n, p = 200, 0.1

print('np      =', n * p)
print('n(1-p)  =', n * (1 - p))
print('safe to approximate?', n * p >= 10 and n * (1 - p) >= 10)

blocks.title: The exact binomial answer
blocks.text: Fewer than 15 no-shows means 14 or fewer. The binomial cdf adds up all fifteen terms for us, so this is the true value we want the normal curve to match.
blocks.code:
from scipy import stats

exact = stats.binom.cdf(14, n, p)

print(f'exact P(X <= 14) = {exact:.4f}')

blocks.title: The normal approximation
blocks.text: Match the normal curve to the binomial's mean np and SD sqrt(np(1 - p)). The continuity correction uses 14.5 because the bar for 14 stretches from 13.5 to 14.5.
blocks.code:
from math import sqrt

mu = n * p
sigma = sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))

with_cc = stats.norm.cdf(14.5, mu, sigma)
without = stats.norm.cdf(14, mu, sigma)

print(f'mu = {mu:.1f}, sigma = {sigma:.3f}')
print(f'normal with correction    = {with_cc:.4f}')
print(f'normal without correction = {without:.4f}')

blocks.title: How close is it?
blocks.text: The error with the half-unit correction is far smaller than without it. That is why the correction matters, even for a big n.
blocks.code:
print(f'error with correction    = {abs(with_cc - exact):.4f}')
print(f'error without correction = {abs(without - exact):.4f}')

r.code:
n <- 200; p <- 0.1
pbinom(14, n, p)
pnorm(14.5, mean = n * p, sd = sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)))
pnorm(14,   mean = n * p, sd = sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)))
r.note: pbinom is the exact answer. The two pnorm lines are the approximation with and without the continuity correction.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (use CDF.BINOM and CDF.NORMAL)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / dummy.
BEGIN DATA
1
END DATA.
COMPUTE exact = CDF.BINOM(14, 200, 0.1).
COMPUTE mu = 200 * 0.1.
COMPUTE sigma = SQRT(200 * 0.1 * 0.9).
COMPUTE with_cc = CDF.NORMAL(14.5, mu, sigma).
COMPUTE without_cc = CDF.NORMAL(14, mu, sigma).
FORMATS exact with_cc without_cc (F8.4).
LIST exact with_cc without_cc.
spss.note: CDF.BINOM(k, n, p) is the exact answer; CDF.NORMAL(value, mean, sd) is the approximation.

stata.code:
display binomial(200, 14, 0.1)
display normal((14.5 - 20) / sqrt(200 * 0.1 * 0.9))
display normal((14 - 20) / sqrt(200 * 0.1 * 0.9))
stata.note: binomial(n,k,p) is the exact P(X <= k). The two normal() lines standardise the cut-off by hand, with and without the half-unit correction.
